key_concept: Aniline ($C_6H_5NH_2$) needs the $-NH_2$ group bonded directly to the ring; this is achieved by Hofmann bromamide degradation of benzamide or by acid hydrolysis of acetanilide, but not by $LiAlH_4$ reduction of a nitrile or $NaBH_4$ treatment of a nitro compound.
steps: A: $C_6H_5C\equiv N \xrightarrow{LiAlH_4} C_6H_5CH_2NH_2$ (benzylamine). The extra $-CH_2-$ means the product is not aniline, so A is incorrect.
B: Hofmann bromamide degradation: $C_6H_5CONH_2 + Br_2 + 4KOH \rightarrow C_6H_5NH_2 + K_2CO_3 + 2KBr + 2H_2O$. The carbonyl carbon is lost, so the product is aniline. B is correct.
C: $NaBH_4$ is a mild hydride donor. It reduces aldehydes and ketones but does not reduce an aromatic $-NO_2$ group to $-NH_2$. Aniline is not the major product, so C is incorrect.
D: Acid hydrolysis of the amide: $C_6H_5NHCOCH_3 + H_2O \xrightarrow{HCl,\Delta} C_6H_5NH_3^+Cl^- + CH_3COOH$. Basifying the anilinium salt gives aniline. D is correct.
So only B and D give aniline. This matches option (2).
why_not_others: Options (1) and (3) include A, but $LiAlH_4$ reduction of benzonitrile gives benzylamine, not aniline. Options (3) and (4) include C, but $NaBH_4$ cannot reduce $-NO_2$ to $-NH_2$; that needs reagents such as $Sn/HCl$, $Fe/HCl$ or $H_2/Pd$.
common_trap: Students treat any reduction of a nitrogen compound as giving aniline, forgetting that nitrile reduction adds a $-CH_2-$ (giving benzylamine) and that $NaBH_4$ is too weak to reduce a nitro group.
time_saving_tip: Recognise B as the classic Hofmann degradation to aniline, then discard A. That leaves only option (2), the single option containing B but not A.
